summary: The recent changes introduce on‑device OCR and a full category‑management system. CSV export now prefixes formula‑triggering characters, fixing the previous CSV‑injection issue. However, the earlier concerns about insufficient category‑name sanitisation and the potential DoS from unbounded receipt‑text parsing remain unresolved. A new medium‑severity issue is introduced: custom category names (and renamed categories) are stored without sanitising control or invisible Unicode characters, which could break UI rendering, CSV/PDF export, or be used for hidden‑character attacks.

findings.issue: `parseReceipt` applies several regular expressions on the raw OCR text without input length limits. An attacker supplying a very large or specially crafted receipt string could cause catastrophic back‑tracking and freeze the UI (ReDoS).
findings.fix: Limit the maximum length of the OCR text processed (e.g., 10 KB) and use non‑catastrophic regex patterns; consider a line‑by‑line parse instead of large global matches.

findings.issue: Category names are only checked for a length of 1‑40 characters, but no sanitisation is performed. Certain Unicode control characters or line‑breaks could break CSV or PDF generation and UI layout.
findings.fix: Trim whitespace, reject control characters (e.g., \n, \r, \t) and normalise Unicode (NFC). Ensure the validated string is safe for all downstream formats.

findings.issue: Custom category names (including renamed categories) are accepted without sanitising Unicode control characters, line‑separator characters, or other non‑printable code points. Such characters can break UI layout, interfere with CSV or PDF generation, and enable hidden‑character attacks.
findings.fix: Validate category strings before storing: trim whitespace, reject or strip characters in Unicode categories Cc, Cf, Zl, Zp (control, format, line/paragraph separators). Apply the same validation to renamed categories. Consider normalising to NFC and limiting to printable characters.
